name: Cenchrus
common_group: sandburs and bristlegrasses (including buffelgrass in modern broad Cenchrus)

project_scope.selection_mode: Existing canonical C. spinifex FINISH/ENRICH; genus comparison only for other Cenchrus species, no first-card admissions
project_scope.native_target_zone_status: NOT_ASSESSED — county BONAP/NAPA or vouchered Texas data required for county-level assertion
project_scope.caution: Some native sandburs and introduced or invasive grasses belong to Cenchrus. Genus recognition does not confer native-range PASS.
project_scope.note: One Cenchrus spinifex species.json already installed and three physical JPGs checked on 2026-10-21. Former zero count was stale. C. longispinus, C. echinatus and 2026 reinstated incertus are comparisons only. Native-by-Hays county unreviewed and original range/science status preserved.

look_here_first: CENCHRUS: sandbur fruit is a bristly FASCICLE enclosing the actual grass spikelets, NOT a naked seed or awn. Three original C. spinifex group photos show the attached burrs; two new CC-licensed comparison photos teach C. longispinus head habit and an actual ruler-scaled dry bur. Both can look alike. Count all coarse and fine bristles and examine the fused cupule of a ripe intact bur. The 2026 Wipff revision resurrected Texas segregates, so don't determine exact species or Hays nativity from a dramatic spine photo.

genus_diagnostics.habit: Annual and perennial grasses; tufted, erect, ascending or sprawling forms. Size and growth form differ substantially among taxa.
genus_diagnostics.leaf: Typical grass node, sheath, blade and collar. Inspect the LIGULE as a hair fringe when visible, but this alone does not diagnose Cenchrus.
genus_diagnostics.inflorescence: Panicle commonly contracted into a dense spike-like array, sometimes with bristly units surrounding spikelets. Bur-bearing species have stiff, sometimes barbed or fused basal bristles that detach as a unit.
genus_diagnostics.spikelet: Each apparent bur or bristly fascicle may contain one or multiple grass spikelets. Separate bristles (modified branch structures) from GLUMES, LEMMAS, and PALEAS.
genus_diagnostics.fruit: Grass caryopsis enclosed in associated spikelet parts; dispersal structures vary by species. Do not treat the whole detachable bur as one naked seed.
genus_diagnostics.taxonomy: Modern broad Cenchrus includes taxa historically placed in Pennisetum. Many non-spiny bottlebrush grasses share the genus, so a painful bur cannot define the entire genus.
genus_diagnostics.bristle_attachment: Observe an entire mature unit from base: inner enclosing bristles may be united into a cupule, shorter outer bristles may be directed backwards, and grass spikelets sit inside. Whole fused fascicle ≠ bare seed.
genus_diagnostics.texas_2026_revision: Wipff (2026, Journal of the Botanical Research Institute of Texas 20:1) reinstates Texas/US taxa previously synonymized with C. spinifex, including C. incertus, and names C. densiflorus from southern Texas. Legacy 'spinifex' source IDs therefore deserve conditional species review, not automated changes to existing taxa/ranges.
genus_diagnostics.classroom_safety: Gloves/forceps and isolated mature bur before dissection. Avoid pressing barbed fascicles into skin.

visual_lesson.status: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — 3 C. spinifex source photos, 2 C. longispinus comparison photos, 14 visible arrows; cupule dissection and 2026 segregate key unresolved
visual_lesson.teaching_order: whole grass with several separate burrs → attached cluster macro → one undamaged ripe detached fascicle → true inner bristle cupule and outer elements → actual 1–4 enclosed spikelets → collar/rooted base → current Texas species-level key

steps.title: 1 · Recognize the bur-bearing grass
steps.photo_role: Existing source labelled sandbur in sandy field, entire grass with narrow blades and more than one fruiting culm
steps.look_for: Discrete spiny round burrs separated along a slender grass inflorescence; the whole grass visible with small sandy clump.

steps.title: 2 · See actual bur spines
steps.photo_role: Existing real green burrs against finger, with several visible separate fascicles on head
steps.look_for: Radiating pointed green outer elements and distinct burr bodies; these are enclosing bristles, not seeds or awns.

steps.title: 3 · Compare a second full head
steps.photo_role: Existing real yellow-green spiny burr groups along flowering branches
steps.look_for: Individual burr units and radiating spine shape; reproductive inner spikelets are not exposed.

steps.title: 4 · Count mature bristles and cupule
steps.photo_role: Detached single intact mature fascicle, with 1-mm scale and base exposed
steps.look_for: Count ALL large AND tiny bristles and measure the broad fused inner bases. Classic regional key: spinifex 8–40, longispinus 45–75; extensive overlap with resurrected 2026 Texan segregates requires current species key.

steps.title: 5 · Expose enclosed true spikelets
steps.photo_role: Forceps-opened full mature bur showing spikelet count and glumes
steps.look_for: Identify the true grass spikelets INSIDE the bristles and any fused cupule; distinguish lower glume, lemma and palea.

steps.title: 6 · Find true ligule
steps.photo_role: True leaf collar/sheath/blade junction under 1-mm ruler
steps.look_for: Hair fringe at ligule is supporting genus context, not sufficient for species distinction.

comparison_cards.title: Cenchrus spinifex group versus C. longispinus — counted mature fascicles
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Longispinus often has MANY more THIN bristles; spinifex sensu older keys tends fewer stouter bristles. Count the whole bur, not just the conspicuous dominant spines.
comparison_cards.field_note: Go Botany's classic key for spinifex gives total 8–40 bristles and broader inner bases ~1–3 mm; longispinus gives 45–75 bristles and narrower bases ~0.5–0.9(–1.4) mm. 2026 Wipff Texas group revision means this two-species comparison does not exhaust regional segregates.
comparison_cards.status: Licensed longispinus exterior photos available; mature full bristle count and species key still missing

field_matrix.character: All burr bristles — not just big spines
field_matrix.spinifex: Typically 8–40 total, often around 6–10 stout dominant spines in some treatments
field_matrix.longispinus: Often 45–75 slender bristles of different lengths

field_matrix.spinifex: Typically 1–3 mm, often broad flattened bristle bases
Texas 2026 spinifex-group resurrected taxa require rekey of a mature voucher
field_matrix.longispinus: Source determination and geography alone not proof; use count and cupule plus key

comparison_cards.photo_evidence: Source-labelled Russian flowering head and source-categorized dry sandspur with centimeter scale. Gross burr structure only; no Texas voucher.

comparison_cards.title: C. spinifex versus C. echinatus and resurrected C. incertus
comparison_cards.look_here_first: These are all potentially spiny burr-bearing sandburs. Separate by the WHOLE mature fascicle, bristle whorls/bases and current Texas species key.
comparison_cards.field_note: Wipff (2026) shows that earlier broad C. spinifex usage covers more than one Texas species. This lesson does not rename current approved card or certify Hays nativity.

comparison_cards.title: Sandburs versus Setaria foxtails
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Hard sandburs enclose spikelets in a coherent spine-and-bristle BUR/CUPULE; ordinary Setaria foxtails have separate softer persistent bristles subtending spikelets along the head.
comparison_cards.caution: Cenchrus in the modern broad genus ALSO includes nonspiny soft-bristled lineages; prickliness cannot delimit the genus.

comparison_cards.title: Field burrs versus a true grass seed/awn
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Pull an undamaged mature bur with forceps, observe the enclosing barbed bristles, then expose true spikelets and their glumes/lemmas. A solid thorn is not an awn and the entire bur is not the caryopsis.

safety_and_field_notes: Wear gloves and use forceps for mature sharp burs; never press a barbed cluster into bare skin.
The WHOLE bur is a bristly fascicle, not a naked seed, and its sharp outer parts are not floral awns.
The visible photo of a hand provides rough context but not a millimeter measurement or license to demonstrate punctures.
Habitat disturbance or prickliness does not automatically establish exotic status. Texas contains native sandburs as well as introduced or invasive Cenchrus.
Wipff's April 2026 taxonomic revision reinstates several C. spinifex-group segregates in Texas; do not declare a source-labelled photo a species-proof identification.
Do not install unrelated hard burr and soft bottlebrush species under the single spinifex name; historic Pennisetum names require synonym checks.
